DOCUMENT:
Business Case: Self-Checkout Expansion
Northfield Grocers, prepared for the Executive Committee, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper asks the Executive Committee to approve capital of £1.34 million to install self-checkout lanes in the 14 Northfield stores that do not yet have them, bringing all 18 stores onto the same front-end format by the end of Q3 2026. The recommendation rests on a ten-month pilot in four stores, which began in May 2025.

2. Background
Front-end labour is our second-largest controllable cost after stock. Staffed checkout hours have risen 9% over two years while transaction counts have been flat, largely because of minimum-wage increases and the difficulty of rostering part-time staff for evening peaks. Queue length is also the most frequent complaint in our customer feedback system, cited in 31% of negative comments in 2025.

The four pilot stores (Ashby, Carrow, Denholme and Wexley) were chosen because they had been fully refurbished in early 2025 and had the floor space to accommodate a six-kiosk bank without removing shelving. Each received six kiosks and retained two staffed lanes.

3. Pilot results
Across the three pilot stores, the key results after ten months were:

Metric | Pilot stores | Other stores
Staffed checkout hours per week (change) | -95 hours per store | +3 hours per store
Average queue time at peak | 2.1 min (from 4.6) | 4.4 min (from 4.5)
Shrink as % of sales | 1.2% (from 1.2%) | 1.3% (from 1.3%)
Average basket value (change) | +6% | +2%
Customer satisfaction, front end (index) | 78 (from 71) | 72 (from 72)

The reduction in staffed hours was achieved without redundancies, through natural turnover and redeployment of colleagues into online order picking. Shrink did not move, which addresses the main concern raised when the pilot was approved. Front-end satisfaction rose seven points in the pilot stores and was flat elsewhere.

The rise in average basket value is the most encouraging result. Basket value grew three times as fast in the pilot stores as in the rest of the estate, which shows that faster, more convenient checkout encourages customers to buy more per visit. We have not built this revenue effect into the financial case below, but it represents meaningful upside.

4. Costs
Kiosks cost £14,500 each including the scanning scale and payment terminal. At six kiosks per store, the hardware cost is £87,000 per store, or £1,218,000 for 14 stores. Installation, electrical work and fit-out are quoted at £9,000 per store, a further £126,000, giving total capital of £1,344,000.

Ongoing maintenance and software licensing are quoted at £4,800 per store per year, or £67,200 across the 14 stores.

5. Savings
We assume each new store achieves the same 95-hour weekly reduction as the pilot stores, which is about 12% of a typical store's front-end hours. At a fully loaded front-end cost of £15.20 per hour, this is £1,444 per store per week, or £75,088 per store per year. Across 14 stores, gross labour savings are £1,051,232 per year.

After maintenance and licensing, net annual savings are £1,118,432. Against capital of £1,344,000, the investment pays back in about 14 months, well inside the group's 24-month hurdle for store equipment.

6. Risks
Supply. The vendor has confirmed lead times of eight weeks, consistent with completion in Q3.

Customer acceptance. Older customers in some rural stores may prefer staffed lanes. Every store will keep at least two staffed lanes, and a colleague will be assigned to the kiosk bank at peak times, as in the pilot.

Labour transition. As in the pilot, reductions will be achieved through turnover and redeployment rather than redundancy. Annual front-end staff turnover across the estate is 38%, well above the 12% reduction in hours required, so we do not expect to need a consultation process.

7. Recommendation
The pilot has shown that self-checkout cuts peak queue times by more than half, holds shrink flat, improves customer satisfaction and lifts basket value, while delivering labour savings that repay the investment in little over a year. We recommend that the Committee approve capital of £1.34 million and a rollout to all 14 remaining stores, sequenced by store size, to complete by the end of September 2026.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "After maintenance and licensing, net annual savings are £1,118,432." -- Maintenance and licensing (£67,200) has been added to gross labour savings (£1,051,232) instead of subtracted. Correct net savings are £1,051,232 - £67,200 = £984,032, so payback on £1,344,000 is about 16.4 months, not 'about 14 months'.
2. [inconsistency] at: "Across the three pilot stores, the key results after ten months were:" -- The document elsewhere says the pilot ran in four stores and names them (Ashby, Carrow, Denholme and Wexley); here the results are attributed to three pilot stores. The pilot store count contradicts itself.
3. [unsupported_causal] at: "Basket value grew three times as fast in the pilot stores as in the rest of the estate, which shows that faster, more convenient checkout encourages customers to buy more per visit." -- Pilot stores were not randomly chosen: the document says they were selected because they had just been fully refurbished in early 2025 (and were larger). Refurbishment and store selection are obvious confounders for basket growth, so the comparison cannot show that self-checkout caused larger baskets.

REVIEW:
# Review: Self-Checkout Expansion Business Case

The case is clearly structured, and the hardware and gross savings arithmetic is correct. However, there is a **calculation error in the headline financials**, an internal inconsistency in the pilot description, and several places where the evidence is presented more strongly than it supports. None of these necessarily overturns the recommendation, but the Committee would likely catch the first two.

## 1. Errors to fix

**Net savings are added instead of subtracted (Section 5).** Maintenance is a cost, so net savings should be:

- £1,051,232 − £67,200 = **£984,032**, not £1,118,432
- Payback: £1,344,000 ÷ £984,032 ≈ 1.37 years, which is **about 16 months**, not 14

This is still well inside the 24-month hurdle, so the conclusion holds. But it is the headline number, and the Recommendation's "little over a year" should change to "about 16 months."

**"Three pilot stores" (Section 3).** The text says "Across the three pilot stores," but Section 2 names four: Ashby, Carrow, Denholme and Wexley. Either this is a typo, or the results exclude one store. If one was excluded, the paper needs to say which and why.

## 2. Claims stronger than the evidence

**Basket value is overclaimed.** The pilot stores were chosen because they had just been fully refurbished. Refurbishment alone commonly lifts basket value and satisfaction. Saying the +6% "shows that faster, more convenient checkout encourages customers to buy more" assigns causation the pilot can't establish. The same confound applies to the 7-point satisfaction rise. I'd suggest:

- Describe both as "consistent with" a self-checkout benefit, while acknowledging the refurbishment.
- Better, compare against other recently refurbished stores if there are any.

The paper is right to exclude basket value from the financial case. It should also stop calling it "the most encouraging result."

**Pilot stores aren't representative, but savings are assumed identical.** The pilot stores were selected for having the floor space to fit six kiosks without removing shelving. The rollout stores were by implication not selected that way. The case then assumes:

- **The same 95-hour reduction in every store.** Smaller or quieter stores will have fewer front-end hours to remove. The plan to sequence by store size suggests sizes vary meaningfully. A per-store estimate, or at least a sensitivity range, would be more credible.
- **Six kiosks per store.** Is this right for every store regardless of size and footfall?
- **The same £9,000 fit-out.** Stores without the spare floor space may need shelving removed. That raises costs and may reduce selling space, a cost the case doesn't mention.

**Shrink.** Ten months of flat shrink in four newly refurbished stores is encouraging. Still, self-checkout shrink often creeps up as regular customers learn the system. It's worth saying the pilot period is relatively short and committing to monitor shrink after rollout.

## 3. Gaps in the financial case

- **No ramp-up.** The 14-month (corrected: 16-month) payback assumes full savings from day one. In practice:
  - Installation is phased through Q3.
  - The labour reduction depends on natural turnover, so hours fall gradually.

  A realistic phasing would push payback out further, though probably still within 24 months.
- **Peak-time kiosk supervisor.** The risks section says a colleague will staff the kiosk bank at peak. Confirm the 95-hour figure is already net of this, as it presumably was in the pilot.
- **No contingency, asset life or depreciation.** Kiosk lifespan and any refresh or replacement cost would round out the case.
- **Sensitivity.** A simple table showing payback at, say, 60 and 80 hours saved per store would make the case much more robust to challenge.

## 4. Risks section

- **Redeployment capacity.** The pilot moved staff into online order picking. Across 14 stores, the reduction is about 1,330 hours per week. Is there enough picking demand to absorb that? If not, the plan leans entirely on turnover, which slows the savings.
- **Turnover vs. reduction.** Comparing 38% turnover with a 12% hours reduction is reasonable at estate level. But turnover isn't evenly spread across stores or timed to match installation. Some stores may still face a shortfall.
- **Customer acceptance.** The rural or older-customer concern hasn't been tested, since the pilot stores appear to be refurbished, larger sites. Say so, or name a pilot store with a comparable demographic if one exists.
- **Supply and installation capacity.** An eight-week lead time covers delivery. Does the installer have capacity for 14 stores in roughly four months?

## 5. Minor points

- The "other stores" comparison shows staffed hours *rising* by 3 per store. So the relative saving is about 98 hours, which slightly supports your case.
- The paper is dated March 2026, with completion targeted for end of Q3 2026, and that date has now passed. If this document is being reused or re-circulated, the timeline will need updating.

## Summary of suggested edits

| Section | Change |
|---|---|
| 3 | "three pilot stores" → "four" (or explain the exclusion) |
| 3 | Soften the basket value and satisfaction claims; note the refurbishment confound |
| 5 | Net savings £984,032; payback ~16 months |
| 5 | Add phasing/ramp-up and a sensitivity range on hours saved |
| 4/5 | Address stores lacking floor space (cost and selling space) |
| 6 | Add redeployment capacity and installer capacity |
| 7 | Update "little over a year" and the basket value claim |
